entry.title: Apache Shiro joins the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund
entry.content:
Apache Shiro is now part of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund. We are glad to be in the company of other widely used projects, and we are grateful to GitHub for supporting the security work that maintainers do.

What the fund does

The fund pairs maintainers with funding, security education and direct access to security experts. The goal is to help projects find and fix vulnerabilities before they reach the people who depend on them.

The agentic security pilot

As part of the fund, GitHub, Microsoft Security and the GitHub Security Lab ran a pilot using Codename MDASH, Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness. The pilot scanned widely used open source projects for security vulnerabilities and worked with maintainers on the fixes.

The emphasis of the pilot is a good fit for our project. Maintainers do not need more AI-generated bug reports. They need fixes that are correct, reviewed and ready to merge. Findings were coordinated with maintainers, so they could be triaged, discussed and shipped through each project’s normal release process.

Read the full write-up, including the combined results across all five sessions of the fund and a video with feedback from participating maintainers, in the GitHub blog post.

What this means for Shiro users

Security reports for Shiro continue to follow the process described in our security policy, and fixes are announced through our usual advisories and releases. Please keep your Shiro dependencies up to date, and see our recent security advisories post for details on current fixes.

Shiro still needs sustained support

The fund is a one-time contribution. It helps us right now, but it does not pay for the ongoing work of reviewing reports, writing fixes, testing and shipping releases. As we described in our community effort post, Shiro is maintained entirely by volunteers, and the project needs continuing support to stay healthy and secure.

If your organization depends on Shiro, please consider helping:

  • Engage a company that offers commercial support for Shiro.

  • Sponsor the maintainers directly on GitHub: Benjamin Marwell and Lenny Primak.

  • See our support page for more ways to give back.

Thank you

Thank you to the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund team, the Microsoft Security and GitHub Security Lab teams, and the other maintainers in the program. We look forward to continuing this work and making Shiro safer for everyone who builds on it.

entry.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): what Shiro users should know
entry.content:
The OpenJDK team has published a security advisory for CVE-2026-114938, also known as Java4Shell. This is a vulnerability in the OpenJDK HotSpot Base64 decoder, not a vulnerability in Apache Shiro itself. Shiro applications can still be vulnerable because Shiro decodes Base64 data using the JDK.

What is affected

The vulnerable code is an optimized Base64 decoding path in HotSpot JVM. Exploitation requires a vulnerable Java runtime and an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. This is a CPU capability, not a condition limited to Intel processors; some AMD processors support it as well. ARM64 systems are not known to be affected.

The Java runtime vendor and version matter. OpenJDK and Oracle have published affected-version details, and other Java distributors may publish their own build-specific guidance. Check the advisory for the vendor and runtime you deploy, including JDKs bundled with applications, containers, and appliances.

How this relates to Shiro

Shiro’s web CookieRememberMeManager Base64-encodes serialized identity data in the remember-me cookie and decodes that cookie when reading it. Shiro’s Base64 decoder delegates to java.util.Base64, so a request handled through this path may be vulnerable.

This does not mean every Shiro deployment is exploitable. Exposure depends on the Java runtime, CPU capabilities, and whether an application reaches the affected decoder path. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and changing Shiro versions alone does not fix a vulnerable JDK.

Remediation

Upgrade to a fixed Java runtime from your distributor as soon as possible. Inventory all JVMs, including those bundled with services and container images, and follow the affected-version and update guidance from the Java vendor. Prioritize internet-facing systems.

Until you can apply the update, the following JVM option mitigates this issue on runtimes that support it:

JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS='-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics' java -jar your-app.jar

For managed services and containers, configure the option on the actual application JVM and restart the service. Treat this as a temporary mitigation, verify that your runtime accepts the option, and still apply the vendor’s fixed runtime update.

Further information

  • OpenJDK Vulnerability Advisory, 2026/11/17

  • Oracle Critical Security Patch Update Advisory, November 2026

  • CISA: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching

  • Java4Shell technical write-up and recommendations

  • Shiro 3.0.2 CookieRememberMeManager

  • Shiro 3.0.2 Base64 codec

The Apache Shiro Team

entry.title: Critical security advisories: LDAP realm and cookie fixes
entry.content:
The Apache Shiro team has published three critical security advisories. Two affect DefaultLdapRealm and one affects the default cookie settings. Please review them and upgrade if you are affected. The full list is on the Vulnerability Reports page.

CVE-2026-129349: any password accepted with LDAP authentication caching

When authentication caching is enabled on DefaultLdapRealm, a user who has logged in successfully once can log in again with any password. A cached authentication skips the LDAP bind, and the AllowAllCredentialsMatcher installed by default accepts any credentials. An attacker who knows a valid username can authenticate as that user.

  • Severity: Critical

  • Affected: all Shiro versions through 3.0.0, only when using DefaultLdapRealm (or JndiLdapRealm) with authenticationCachingEnabled set to true. This is not the default.

  • Fix: upgrade to 3.0.1 or later. AllowAllCredentialsMatcher is no longer installed by default.

  • Workarounds: keep authentication caching disabled on the LDAP realm (the default), or configure a credentials matcher such as SimpleCredentialsMatcher that verifies credentials against the cached authentication info.

  • Credit: thanks to Joshua Rogers for reporting this issue.

CVE-2026-49268: LDAP DN injection in DefaultLdapRealm

A remote attacker can inject LDAP special characters into the Distinguished Name (DN) built by DefaultLdapRealm. The username was concatenated into the DN template without escaping the RFC 2253 special characters. This lets an attacker change the DN structure used for the LDAP bind, which can bypass authentication or impersonate other users.

  • Severity: Critical

  • Affected: all Shiro versions through 2.2.0, and 3.0.0-alpha-1, when using DefaultLdapRealm.

  • Fix: upgrade to 2.2.1, or 3.0.0-alpha-2 or later. User-supplied DN values are now escaped.

  • Credit: thanks to zhaokaifei for reporting this issue.

CVE-2026-43828: session cookies sent without the Secure attribute

By default, the Shiro-native session manager and the Remember-Me manager sent the JSESSIONID and rememberMe cookies without the Secure attribute, even over HTTPS.

  • Severity: Critical

  • Affected: Shiro 1.0 to 2.1.0, and 3.0.0-alpha-1.

  • Fix: upgrade to 2.2.0, or 3.0.0-alpha-2 or later. The Secure attribute is now set.

  • Credit: thanks to Meteor_Kai for reporting this issue.

What you should do

  • Upgrade to the latest release listed on the download page. Version 3.0.2 or later covers all three issues on the 3.x line, and 2.2.1 or later covers them on the 2.x line.

  • Review your LDAP realm configuration, especially if authentication caching is enabled.

  • Check that your session and Remember-Me cookies carry the Secure attribute.

If you find a security issue, please report it by following the instructions on the Vulnerability Reports page.

The Apache Shiro Team

entry.title: 3.0.2 available
entry.content:
The Apache Shiro team is pleased to announce the release of Apache Shiro version 3.0.2.

This release is available for download now.

Release Highlights

This is a maintenance release with security fixes, a new feature, and a number of improvements and bug fixes. It is recommended that all users upgrade to this version.

New Features

  • Form data can now be saved and replayed without requiring a sign-in page

Security Fixes

  • Superclass and interface annotation processing is harmonized across integrations

  • Default settings of ShiroFilterFactoryBean and NoAccessFilter are now aligned with other components

  • Many more hardening and security improvements have been made throughout the framework (see Vulnerability Reports).

Improvements

This release includes various improvements to form data saving and replay, Spring Boot 4.2+ support, logging, SBOM generation, and build and CI stability.

Bug Fixes

This release includes several bug fixes in Spring configuration, permission handling, and Faces form replay.

Migration Guide

If you are upgrading from an earlier version of Shiro, please read the Migration Guide for important changes and upgrade instructions.

Thank you to the following contributors!

  • Sharang Gupta (first contribution)

  • Nexory

  • BalusC

  • John Bampton

Release Notes

The full list of changes is available on GitHub, Release 3.0.2.

Download

Download and verification instructions are available on our download page.

Documentation

For more information on Shiro, please read the documentation.

Enjoy!

The Apache Shiro Team

entry.content:
The Apache Shiro team is pleased to announce the release of Apache Shiro version 3.0.1.

This release is available for download now.

Release Highlights

This is a maintenance release that includes several security enhancements and bug fixes. It is recommended that all users upgrade to this version.

Security Enhancements

  • Case-insensitive filters are now the default for programmatic and Spring / Spring Boot configurations

  • RememberMe deserialization has been hardened

  • Guice and AOP annotation retrieval has been improved to prevent potential security issues

  • Active Directory DN authentication has been fixed to prevent potential security issues

  • Jakarta EE form resubmit security has been enhanced

entry.title: 3.0.0 available
entry.content:
The Apache Shiro team is pleased to announce the release of Apache Shiro version 3.0.0.

This release is available for download now.

Release Highlights

This is a new major release of Apache Shiro, with many new features and improvements, culminating more than two years of work.

  • JDK 17 is the new minimum baseline

  • Jakarta EE 9/10/11+ (no javax.* namespace)

  • Spring 6/7+ and SpringBoot 3/4+

  • Guice 7/8+

  • Using Java Scoped values for Subject and SecurityManager instead of ThreadLocals on JDK 25+

  • Improved thread-safety of Shiro-native sessions (SimpleSession, SimpleSessionFactory, CachingSessionDAO)

Breaking API Changes

  • Made default implementation of PrincipalCollection immutable (ImmutablePrincipalCollection)

Security Enhancements

  • Case-insensitive path matching is now enabled by default (hardened by default)

  • Added NoAccessFilter and add it to the default filter chain (breaking change, hardened-by-default)

  • Enable CORS preflight requests by default

End-of-life notice

Apache Shiro 1.x and 2.x are now considered end-of-life. If support for these versions is required, please check Commercial Support

Thank you to the following contributors!

  • Martin Geisse

  • Tim te Beek

  • Rui Ventura

  • Patrick (Gus) Heck

All changes

You can learn more on GitHub, Release 3.0.0.

Download

Download and verification instructions are available on our download page.

Documentation

For more information on Shiro, please read the documentation.

Enjoy!

The Apache Shiro Team

entry.title: Apache Shiro: A New Chapter Driven by Community
entry.content:
Apache Shiro has entered a new chapter, one filled with opportunity.

For years, Shiro has quietly powered authentication, authorization, cryptography, and session management for countless applications around the world. Its simplicity and flexibility made it a favorite among developers who needed security without unnecessary complexity.

Today, with the conclusion of past corporate sponsorships of Shiro’s individual contributors, the project is maintained entirely by dedicated volunteers who believe in its mission and its value to the ecosystem.

Open source has always thrived because of community support. Some of the most resilient and innovative projects exist because individuals and organizations stepped up when it mattered most. Shiro is now at that moment.

Why This Matters

  • Shiro remains a critical dependency for many production systems

  • Its lightweight, framework-agnostic design fills a unique niche

  • Continued maintenance ensures security, stability, and trust

What’s Needed Now

  • Contributors to help with development, testing, and documentation

  • Organizations willing to financially sponsor ongoing work via commercial support

  • Advocates who believe in sustainable open source

If you rely on Shiro, even indirectly, this is the time to invest in its future. Financial involvement isn’t just support; it’s a way to ensure the tools you depend on remain secure, modern, and well-maintained.

And if you’re an engineer looking to make an impact, this is a rare chance to shape the direction of a widely used security framework.

Open source doesn’t disappear when funding changes, it evolves based on who shows up next.

Let’s make sure Shiro continues to be a project worth relying on.

What you can do right now

  • Consider commercial support for the project to ensure its sustainability

  • Contribute code, tests, or documentation

  • Spread the word

entry.title: 3.0.0-alpha-1 available
entry.content:
The Apache Shiro team is pleased to announce the release of Apache Shiro version 3.0.0-alpha-1.

This release is available for download now.

Release Highlights

  • Java 17 is the minimum requirement

  • Using Scoped values instead of ThreadLocals on JDK 25+

  • Jakarta EE 11, Spring 7 and SpringBoot 4 without classifiers, dropped support for Jakarta EE 8, SpringBoot 2 and javax namespace

  • Removed many deprecations

  • Refactored code to use Java 17+ features

The reason this is still an Alpha release is because we are still unsure of further API stability, but the release is in a good enough state to try out with your current projects.
